facts: Velocity is the derivative of position: $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)=\dot{x}(t)\underset{\sim}{i}+\dot{y}(t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=\ddot{x}(t)\underset{\sim}{i}+\ddot{y}(t)\underset{\sim}{j}$.
Differentiate the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ components separately, because $\underset{\sim}{i}$ and $\underset{\sim}{j}$ are constant.
**Speed** is the size of the velocity, $|\underset{\sim}{v}|=\sqrt{\dot{x}^{2}+\dot{y}^{2}}$, so it is never negative.
Speed is not $\dot{x}+\dot{y}$: square the components, add, then take the square root.
The velocity vector points along the tangent to the particle's path at that instant.
Velocity and acceleration need not point the same way; in circular motion they are perpendicular.
To find velocity or acceleration at $t=a$, differentiate first and substitute afterwards.
steps: Write the components $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ of the position vector
Differentiate each component of $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$ to get $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$
Substitute the required value of $t$, and take a magnitude if speed is asked for

foundation.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(3t^{2}-2t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{3}+5)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=4t\underset{\sim}{i}+(16t-5t^{2})\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{3}-4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(2t^{2}+t)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2t^{4}\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{3}-6t)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}+3t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{3}-t)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its velocity when $t=2$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\dfrac{t^{3}}{3}\underset{\sim}{i}+(4t-t^{2})\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its velocity when $t=3$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=t^{2}\underset{\sim}{i}+8t\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its speed when $t=3$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=5t^{2}\underset{\sim}{i}+12t\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its speed when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

development.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=3\cos 2t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+3\sin 2t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^{2t}\underset{\sim}{i}+\ln(t+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$. Find $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=te^{-t}\underset{\sim}{i}+(t^{2}+1)\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its velocity when $t=0$.

development.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=-12\sin 3t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+12\cos 3t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$|\underset{\sim}{v}(t)|$
$=\sqrt{144\sin^{2}3t+144\cos^{2}3t}$
$=\sqrt{144(\sin^{2}3t+\cos^{2}3t)}$
$=\sqrt{144}$
$=12$
The speed does not depend on $t$, so it is constant at $12$.

development.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$. Show that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$ and that $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{v}$.
development.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=-2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$
$=-2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}-2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=-\left(2\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}\right)$
$=-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$
$\underset{\sim}{v}\cdot\underset{\sim}{a}$
$=(-2\sin t)(-2\cos t)+(2\cos t)(-2\sin t)$
$=4\sin t\cos t-4\sin t\cos t$
$=0$
The dot product is zero, so $\underset{\sim}{a}$ is perpendicular to $\underset{\sim}{v}$.

development.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{3}-6t^{2})\underset{\sim}{i}+\dfrac{t^{4}}{4}\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$. Find $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$, and find the time at which the $\underset{\sim}{i}$ component of the acceleration is zero.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=2\sin \pi t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+(3-t^{2})\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its velocity when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=24t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+(26t-4t^{2})\underset{\sim}{j}$. Find its speed when $t=2$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=\dfrac{t}{t+1}\underset{\sim}{i}+\sqrt{4t+1}\,\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$. Find $\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$.

mastery.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}+at)\underset{\sim}{i}+bt^{3}\underset{\sim}{j}$, where $a$ and $b$ are constants. Given that $\underset{\sim}{v}(1)=5\underset{\sim}{i}+6\underset{\sim}{j}$, find $a$ and $b$.
A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=(t^{2}-4t)\underset{\sim}{i}+3t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$ for $t\ge 0$. Find the minimum speed of the particle and the time at which it occurs.
mastery.solution_text:
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)$
$=(2t-4)\underset{\sim}{i}+3\underset{\sim}{j}$
$|\underset{\sim}{v}|^{2}$
$=(2t-4)^{2}+9$
The square root is increasing, so the speed is least when $(2t-4)^{2}$ is least.
$(2t-4)^{2}=0$
$t=2$
$|\underset{\sim}{v}(2)|$
$=\sqrt{0+9}$
$=3$
The minimum speed is $3$, at $t=2$.

mastery.question_text: A particle has position vector $\underset{\sim}{r}(t)=e^{t}\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+e^{t}\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$. Show that $\underset{\sim}{a}(t)=2\left(\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)\right)$.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dot{x}$
$=e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t$
$\dot{y}$
$=e^{t}\sin t+e^{t}\cos t$
$\ddot{x}$
$=(e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t)+(-e^{t}\sin t-e^{t}\cos t)$
$=-2e^{t}\sin t$
$\ddot{y}$
$=(e^{t}\sin t+e^{t}\cos t)+(e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t)$
$=2e^{t}\cos t$
$\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)$
$=(e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t-e^{t}\cos t)\underset{\sim}{i}+(e^{t}\sin t+e^{t}\cos t-e^{t}\sin t)\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=-e^{t}\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+e^{t}\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$2\left(\underset{\sim}{v}(t)-\underset{\sim}{r}(t)\right)$
$=-2e^{t}\sin t\,\underset{\sim}{i}+2e^{t}\cos t\,\underset{\sim}{j}$
$=\underset{\sim}{a}(t)$
